issues.legal_issue: For a development scheme requiring government sanction, the prospective site is identified for environmental-clearance purposes when the scheme is finalized, not when a preliminary notification first identifies the land.
material_facts: A development authority issued a preliminary notification identifying land for the proposed road and inviting objections before the scheme received government sanction.
The scheme could be modified, abandoned, or denied sanction after the preliminary notification, and only after sanction was a final notification issued carrying the scheme into effect.
The final notification for the project was issued after the 2006 environmental-clearance notification came into force.
issues.conclusion: The project commenced for environmental-clearance purposes when the final notification was issued after government sanction; the claim that it commenced with the earlier preliminary notification was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Paragraph 2 of the 2006 EIA Notification requires an application after identification of the prospective site and before construction or land preparation. Sections 17, 18 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Authority Act distinguish the preliminary notification and objection process from government sanction and the final notification that makes the scheme operative. Treating the preliminary notification as identification would require an assessment even for a scheme that might never be approved or carried out.

predicates.environmental_clearance_site_identificat: The proceeding concerns when a proposed development project is treated as having identified its site for environmental-clearance purposes.
predicates.project_requires_statutory_scheme_approv: The project must pass through a statutory process in which government approval is needed before the scheme is finalized and carried out.
predicates.preliminary_notice_precedes_final_scheme: The project authority gives an early notice identifying proposed land before the scheme receives final government approval.

issues.definition: When an environmental-clearance site-identification dispute involves a project requiring statutory scheme approval, and the early land notice precedes final approval, the site is treated as identified when final approval takes effect.

issues.legal_issue: A road designed and operated as an expressway falls within the highway category requiring prior environmental clearance even if it has not been formally notified as a highway under road-specific legislation.
material_facts: The project was a new, divided, multi-lane road designed for high-speed traffic, with controlled access, grade-separated interchanges and toll booths.
The road was intended to carry intercity traffic and decongest urban roads, and access was restricted to specified classes of roads.
The project proponent's own assessment described the project as a new state highway requiring environmental clearance.
The road had not been notified as a highway under the national or state highway enactments.
issues.conclusion: The project was an expressway within paragraph 7(f) of the Schedule to the 2006 EIA Notification and required prior environmental clearance.
issues.legal_principle: Paragraph 2 and paragraph 7(f) of the Schedule to the 2006 EIA Notification require prior environmental clearance for listed highway projects. The 1 December 2009 amendment clarified that highways include expressways. A clarificatory amendment applies retrospectively; the Court relied on State Bank of India v V. Ramakrishnan and the principle stated in G.P. Singh's Principles of Statutory Interpretation. The Indian Roads Congress description of an expressway, including high-speed divided carriageways and control of access, was instructive, with classification assessed case by case.

rule.if: environmental_clearance_applicability_case and road_is_divided_high_speed_route and access_is_controlled and (toll_facilities_exist or grade_separated_interchanges_exist)

predicates.environmental_clearance_applicability_ca: The proceeding concerns whether a road project must obtain prior environmental clearance.
predicates.road_is_divided_high_speed_route: The proposed road has divided carriageways and is designed to carry traffic at high speeds.
predicates.access_is_controlled: Entry to the road is restricted rather than freely available at points along its route.
predicates.toll_facilities_exist: The proposed road includes facilities for collecting tolls from road users.
predicates.grade_separated_interchanges_exist: The proposed road includes grade-separated interchanges at intersections.

issues.definition: When an environmental-clearance applicability dispute concerns a divided high-speed road with controlled access and toll facilities or grade-separated interchanges, the road is treated as an expressway requiring prior clearance.

issues.legal_issue: An environmental-clearance appraisal cannot rely on an expired terms of reference and outdated baseline data when the required assessment has not been completed afresh within the applicable validity period.
material_facts: The terms of reference were issued on 21 November 2009, before the Ministry's 22 March 2010 memorandum prescribing the applicable validity period for earlier terms of reference.
The primary environmental data was collected between December 2009 and February 2010.
The public hearing took place in February 2014, and the assessment report based on the old data was submitted in 2014, after the terms of reference had expired.

Although some additional samples were provided in response to questions from the appraisal committee, they addressed only limited points and did not replace a complete assessment using contemporary data.
The appraisal committee nevertheless considered the report and recommended clearance.
issues.conclusion: The assessment report was prepared on the basis of expired terms of reference and outdated primary data, could not support a valid clearance, and should not have been considered in place of a fresh assessment.
issues.legal_principle: The 22 March 2010 memorandum required reports under pre-existing terms of reference to be submitted within four years and required primary data not older than three years. The 22 August 2014 memorandum required a new process when the terms of reference expired and barred further extension beyond the outer limit. The 7 November 2014 memorandum permitted consideration of certain reports with data older than three years where the terms of reference remained valid, but retained the requirement for a fresh process after expiry. The time limits reflect the dynamic nature of environmental conditions and the need for a contemporary assessment under the 2006 EIA Notification.

rule.if: environmental_clearance_appraisal_case and terms_of_reference_expired_before_final_report and baseline_data_outdated_at_final_report and no_complete_fresh_assessment_was_done

predicates.environmental_clearance_appraisal_case: The proceeding concerns whether an environmental-clearance appraisal was validly conducted for a proposed project.
predicates.terms_of_reference_expired_before_final_: The project proponent submitted the final assessment after the validity period of the instructions governing that assessment had ended.
predicates.baseline_data_outdated_at_final_report: The assessment relied on environmental data that was no longer within the applicable validity period when the final report was prepared.
predicates.no_complete_fresh_assessment_was_done: The project proponent did not conduct a complete new assessment using contemporary data, even if limited additional samples or clarifications were later supplied.

issues.definition: When an environmental-clearance appraisal relies on expired assessment instructions and outdated baseline data without a complete fresh assessment, that assessment cannot support clearance.

issues.legal_issue: An environmental impact assessment for a sector-specific project must be prepared by a consultant accredited for that sector.
material_facts: The project was a highway project, and its final assessment report was prepared by a consultant accredited in other sectors but not for highway projects.
The Ministry's accreditation process confined consultants to the sectors for which they had received accreditation.
The Court directed that the fresh assessment use a sector-specific accredited consultant.
issues.conclusion: The fresh assessment must be prepared by a consultant accredited for highway projects.
issues.legal_principle: The Ministry's 2 December 2009 memorandum required EIA consultants to be registered under the National Accreditation Board for Education and Training and Quality Council of India's accreditation scheme and confined consultants to their accredited sectors. The stated purpose was to improve the quality and specificity of assessment reports and ensure suitable expertise and facilities.

predicates.sector_specific_environmental_assessment: The proceeding concerns the adequacy of an environmental assessment for a project in a defined sector.
predicates.project_belongs_to_a_defined_sector: The proposed project falls within a sector for which consultants may receive distinct accreditation.
predicates.consultant_lacks_accreditation_for_that_: The consultant who prepared the assessment was not accredited to assess projects in the sector to which the project belongs.

issues.definition: When a project belongs to a defined sector and its assessment was prepared by a consultant lacking accreditation for that sector, the assessment must use a sector-accredited consultant.

issues.legal_issue: A project proponent cannot cure contradictory or inadequate disclosure of forest diversion by offering alternative land for afforestation in place of following the required forest-clearance process.
material_facts: The assessment stated both that no forest land was involved and that forest land would be diverted for the project.
The proponent later confirmed that forest land would be diverted but did not provide the required forest clearance with its environmental-clearance material.
Instead, the proponent offered other land for afforestation and gave inconsistent explanations about the status of its dealings with the forest department.
The appraisal committee proceeded to recommend clearance despite the contradictions and the absence of adequate reasons for dispensing with forest clearance.
issues.conclusion: The alternative afforestation land and later explanations did not cure the failure to disclose forest diversion and comply with the prescribed forest-clearance process; the appraisal committee's recommendation was unsustainable.
issues.legal_principle: The Ministry's 31 March 2011 memorandum required a project involving forest land to provide the requisite stage-I forest clearance with its environmental-clearance proposal or to remove the forest land from the proposal. The 9 September 2011 and 18 May 2012 memoranda required disclosure to the appraisal committee of the status of the forest-clearance application and prescribed the process for obtaining and submitting that clearance. A project proponent cannot replace that process with an ad hoc post facto arrangement for afforestation.

predicates.environmental_clearance_forest_land_case: The proceeding concerns environmental clearance for a project that may affect forest land.
predicates.forest_diversion_is_involved: The proposed project requires forest land to be diverted or used.
predicates.forest_diversion_is_not_candidly_disclos: The assessment contains contradictory or materially inadequate information about the forest land affected by the project.
predicates.alternative_afforestation_is_offered_ins: The proponent offers replacement land or afforestation as a substitute for completing the prescribed forest-clearance process.

issues.definition: When a project involves forest diversion, the assessment does not candidly disclose it, and alternative afforestation is offered instead of required clearance, the alternative does not cure the noncompliance.

issues.legal_issue: Materially understating the number of trees to be felled in an environmental impact assessment is a serious disclosure deficiency that undermines environmental appraisal.
material_facts: The assessment stated that only about 519 trees would be felled for the project.
Information from the relevant forestry authority indicated that approximately 16,785 trees were proposed to be cut.
The proponent acknowledged that the assessment's information about tree cutting required correction and relied on later explanations and an alternative afforestation proposal.
The appraisal process did not adequately address the discrepancy before recommending clearance.
issues.conclusion: The failure to disclose the number of trees proposed to be felled was a serious lacuna in the assessment and appraisal process.
issues.legal_principle: The 2006 EIA Notification establishes a process intended to make environmental decision-making transparent, responsive and inclusive through disclosure, assessment, consultation and appraisal. The Court held that concealing significant environmental impacts from scrutiny is not an acceptable means of securing project approval.

predicates.environmental_clearance_disclosure_case: The proceeding concerns whether environmental impacts were properly disclosed and considered in an assessment for clearance.
predicates.project_requires_substantial_tree_fellin: The proposed project requires the felling of a substantial number of trees.
predicates.assessment_materially_understates_tree_f: The assessment reports a materially smaller number of trees to be felled than the available information indicates.
predicates.appraisal_does_not_resolve_the_discrepan: The appraisal body recommends a decision without adequately resolving the material difference in the reported tree-felling figures.

issues.definition: When a project requires substantial tree felling, its assessment materially understates that impact, and the appraisal does not resolve the difference, the nondisclosure is a serious appraisal deficiency.

issues.legal_issue: An expert appraisal committee must scrutinize the assessment and relevant material and give specific reasons for recommending environmental clearance.
material_facts: The appraisal committee had identified deficiencies in the assessment, including issues concerning forest land, environmental data and other project impacts.
Its recommendation relied on the proponent's responses and listed undertakings, without explaining how the deficiencies had been resolved or why clearance was justified.
The regulatory authority would normally accept the committee's recommendation, and the recommendation's reasons would inform any challenge before the environmental tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The committee's cursory recommendation, which did not disclose cogent reasons or demonstrate proper scrutiny, suffered from non-application of mind and vitiated the clearance process.
issues.legal_principle: The 2006 EIA Notification requires detailed appraisal and categorical recommendations supported by reasons; paragraph 8(ii) provides that the regulatory authority shall normally accept the expert committee's recommendations. Section 16 of the National Green Tribunal Act 2010 makes the clearance decision appealable, giving the committee's reasons significance for review. The Court relied on Shreeranganathan K.P. v Union of India concerning proper appraisal of available materials and objections, and Lafarge Umiam Mining Private Limited v Union of India concerning fair, informed and legally principled environmental decision-making.

rule.if: environmental_clearance_appraisal_case and expert_committee_must_review_assessment and committee_does_not_scrutinize_relevant_material and committee_gives_no_cogent_reasons

predicates.environmental_clearance_appraisal_case: The proceeding concerns an expert committee's appraisal of a project seeking environmental clearance.
predicates.expert_committee_must_review_assessment: The appraisal committee is responsible for examining the assessment and other relevant project materials before making a recommendation.
predicates.committee_does_not_scrutinize_relevant_m: The committee fails to meaningfully assess material environmental issues, deficiencies, or objections before it.
predicates.committee_gives_no_cogent_reasons: The committee's recommendation does not explain why clearance is justified or how significant deficiencies were addressed.

issues.definition: When an expert committee responsible for environmental appraisal fails to scrutinize relevant material and gives no cogent reasons, its recommendation vitiates the clearance process.

issues.legal_issue: A road project that may cross a petroleum pipeline must be planned with consultation and precautions sufficient to prevent damage to the pipeline.
material_facts: The proposed road crossed an existing petroleum pipeline at several locations.
The pipeline operator warned that the pipeline carried hazardous and highly inflammable material and sought safeguards.
The project authority and pipeline operator had discussed crossing arrangements, including elevated crossings and restrictions on supports in the pipeline's right of way.
issues.conclusion: The project proponent was directed to consult the appropriate authority to ensure that the project would not cause potential damage to the petroleum pipelines.
issues.legal_principle: The Court issued the direction under Article 142 of the Constitution, taking account of the identified pipeline risk and the need to ensure that the proposed infrastructure project did not damage the hazardous pipeline. The judgment does not identify a separate statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this direction.

predicates.environmental_clearance_infrastructure_c: The proceeding concerns environmental clearance for a proposed infrastructure project.
predicates.project_may_cross_hazardous_pipeline: The proposed project may cross or otherwise affect a pipeline carrying hazardous material.

issues.definition: When an infrastructure project may cross a hazardous pipeline, the project proponent must consult the appropriate authority to prevent pipeline damage.
